blocks.x: Okay, you can give your name if you wish.
My name is Albert French.
And we're having this interview. This is Bill Russell interviewing Mr. French up at his home at 2722 Roberts Street on August 3rd, 1960. Could you tell us just when you were born and where?
I was born in 1910, November 16th, in New Orleans. Right in the city? Right in the city of New Orleans, on Green Street.
And your family, I know your uncle, your uncle Morris French is up?
Up in Laplace.
Up in Laplace. I thought maybe you all came from up that direction.

No, my daddy came from Laplace and my uncle. My dad also played music too. Could you tell us about your father? My father, his name is Bob French, but they call him Bab. Some people call him Bab French. And he played with Kid René. What instrument did he play? He played bass tuba.
Bass tuba.
Bass tuba. He played with a lot of the bands around here.
I'd heard that one member of the family, I didn't know it was your father who it was.
That's my father and I have an uncle in the Baton Rouge, Johnny French. He's a trumpet player.
Is he still living?
He's still living.
Is your father by any chance?
No, my father died in 1925.
Sorry. Can you tell us some more about your father, where he learned and what kind of a band he
played in? Well, my father, most of the band he played, he played with the brass band. And he learned from old man Perkins. Old man Perkins was his teacher.
Dave Perkins.
Dave Perkins. Dave Perkins taught him. I took some lessons from Dave Perkins myself.
Did your father come down here then to study?
My father was staying out here then when he took lessons from Dave Perkins. But he'd learn how to play in the brass band after he got here he started learning music.
Can you give us a few dates about your father? You mentioned when he died and do you remember how old he was then or that'll tell when he was born?
Oh, I think he was just about forty-eight to fifty years old when he died.
Wasn't very old then at all?
No, he wasn't very young. He'd be around the age of some of the older musicians. Such as Papa Celestine and like Prince Bacturo and a lot of old old records, a lot of old timers.
And he started on trumpet? Was that his main instrument all his life?
No, no tubas. He started on tubas. That's your other uncle. Johnny French played trumpet. Yeah, his trumpet player.
Was he older than your father?
No, my father was the oldest boy. My father was the oldest boy.
And who was next?
Your uncle Morris? No, Johnny was next. And then Morris and then he had another brother that's younger. He doesn't play the music.
Doesn't play the music. We have an interview with your uncle Morris. You did? Dick Allen was up and saw him. Fine. Oh, about three weeks ago or so.
Good.
So we're anxious then to hear a little bit more about your father. If you can think of anything else of the bands that he played in?

Well, the bands he played in, I know he played with Tuxedo once. And I think during that time they had the Eureka band and whatnot. He played with a lot of the brass bands I mean because anyone would call him, just like musicians do now, for the brass bands sometimes when the men may be sick or whatnot and then they'd go and play in his place.
Did he play any dance work?
He played dance work. He played at the Bulls. You remember the Bulls?
Same as the Elks Club now.

That's right. He played at the Bulls and he played at the Bulls for years. And I can remember hearing him. Whose band was that? That was Kid Renny's band. Oh, it was Kid Renny. Kid Renny. He played with Kid Renny. And I can remember when I was a little kid I can remember sitting on the steps and the Bulls was about ten blocks from us. And you could hear him play at the Bulls when the wind was blowing back on Sixth Street. And he used to play parades and we used to follow him along the streets. Just like you do, just like the parades now. I mean it's second line and whatnot. We used to go out there and holler, that's my daddy playing bass tube and whatnot. And it was real good. I mean it's just like the days now. I think those days might have been a little better. I'm not sure.
I think so too from what I've seen too.
Some of those older bands probably. Older bands, yeah. It was a lot better.
Did he play E flat or B flat? Do you remember? Was it a big sousaphone that wrapped around or what kind of a horn?

No, it was a straight. It's a straight upright. Straight upright bass. I think it was E flat. E flat or B flat. I just remember what one it is. I had the instrument and I gave it to one of my cousins out in the country. It still had the instrument. They still play it? They still play it. They have a band around Laplace.
Did your father ever go back up there to play then much?
No, well he used to go up there and play dances, different dances like the band leave out of town and play different dates.
But not with any of the local groups up there?
Not with any local groups. Just after he got here with Randy and then we stayed in town and played with the local

bands in New Orleans. Can you tell us anything about your Uncle Morris as you remember him? Naturally we have interviewed directly with him but still if you have any other recollections of him when he was young because some things he might neglect to tell you know sometimes.

Well I can remember Morris from a long time back when I was a kid. And he played, most of the bands he played, he played with Randy for I guess about 20 years or maybe better. Randy was his regular band. He played with some other band but.
At the same time as your father?

At the same time they were both in the same band. And I can remember him a long time ago when they had, I can remember Back Forge when they had the horse and wagon and they used to come, the band used to ride on the street advertising. And as they get on the corner one band would stop and play on the corner, then another band would pull up and play on the corner. Well then they'd be bucking against each other. And the band that leaves the first, well that was the band that lost the contest. But it wasn't all the time that that band lost the contest. The band might have been late getting back in to their place and so they had to leave you see. But I used to look for it every Sunday for the band to come on the corner and advertise. That was the regular thing on Sunday.
Yeah I've heard about that. I've heard that Renee did a lot of that too.
He did. He was. He was.
He was. And you remember anything about Renee's style when you heard it as you remember him playing? I've heard he played high notes but I wondered if you could tell anything else about his style.
Well I'll tell you who's closer to his style now I think, so my idea is this. That's all right. Just take your time.
What is this band? Shulky. Shulky.

Shulky. Well a couple of other people mentioned it. I was going to ask if it was Shulky. If you listen to Shulky. If you listen to Shulky you hear Renee. People tell me he used to follow the band around.
That's right. Shulky did. And Shulky picked up Renee's style.

But I never heard, he never played such high notes actually. No but he just, he played, Renee was a little higher but the same style that Shulky had, Renee had that same style. When you hear Shulky you hear Renee. It's really true. It's really true that Shulky played just like Renee, kid Renee. I think they, I don't know if Renee taught him or what but I know every time Renee would play his job Shulky would be around.

I think somebody did say he almost took lessons, at least they used to follow the band around. That's right. Shulky did. I think somebody said he maybe even took a couple of lessons or something from him.
I think he did because Shulky had the same style. Anytime Shulky played he'd just say that's Renee played because it sounded just the same
thing. You remember who else was in the band when your father and uncle were in the band?

In the Renee's band? Let's see who was in the band. There was a banjo player, Chester Jones I know the bass player was in the band. Chester Jones was one and Zeb the Klanet player. Zeb. You might have heard talk about Zeb.
I think Chester Jones the one I know is a drummer. No it was Chester Zarder.
Oh Zarder. Chester Zarder. That was the bass player. Oh yes I know him too. And you had Renee and you had Morris and you had my daddy and you had the drummer. The drummer was Renee's brother.
Oh yes Joe, I've met him. Joe Renee.
Joe Renee was the drummer.
He's a preacher now up on Jackson.
That's right. Well that was the band during those days. They had a very fine band.
Can you tell us anymore, don't interrupt you, while I think of it though, about Zeb? Because we hardly know his name. I never met him. He's before one of the time.

Well I remember Zeb from a little kid because he used to come home all the time. And Zeb was one of the fine client that player. That's what I hear he must have been good. He stayed with Renee for years.
Do you know how much older he was than you for instance? Do you know when he died or anything about him? Where he came from?

No, I think Zeb came from St. John's Pass. I'm not sure. But Zeb and my daddy, they were around the same age. Right now they'll be around about 80 years old. I figured they'd be around 80 years old. And Zeb, I mean pretty near all the fellas, he wasn't playing with Renee, he'd be playing with some band or another. He was a very fine client player.
See I guess Renee wouldn't be quite that old. He was just a couple years older than Louie.
I figured Renee would be around, I'll say about 65 now. Probably. Just about 65.
Louie's 60. Did you see him on television last night? No I missed him. On the educational station.
Oh, I missed that. That's why, but I'm not looking at the educational station.
It's 9.30, a nice interview. It's only the first part, they're going to have two or three more parts that somebody told me.
What night will he come on?
Tuesday nights. Tuesday nights. The Loyola station I think.
Well I'll look for that.
I'm not sure if it's next week or when it'll be, if the next part may be next week.
Well I'll look for that because I love Louie.
He didn't play, he just talked, told about the old times here.
Well I love Louie because I remember a long time ago when Louie played a lot of records out of the youngster and I used to try to imitate Louie. I had him pretty close. On what?
On singing. On singing. I used to imitate him quite a lot on singing. I didn't know if you were trying to play trumpet the most of the day.
No, I still, well I still was playing the ukulele there.
We'll get into details about your life in a few minutes but while I still think I would let's ask some more about your Uncle Morris. Remember he was born up? He was born in Laplace.
Morris was born in Laplace.
And did he come down here about the same time as your father would you say?
I think they both came down around the same time.
Of course you might not, that was before you were born I guess anyway, wasn't it?

I think it was before I was born because when they came down it was before I was born because I was born here and well I just found out about where they're home was I mean about ten or twelve years after I was born.
Remember anything else about your Uncle Morris where he played or other bands besides Rene that he might have played in?

Well. Some of the bands, I know he played with one band up in Monroe, Taft Kroon, I know he played with Taft Kroon. And well he played with Rene and I think at times he used to play with Jack Carey. You remember Jack Carey? Yeah. Well sometimes he used to use two trombones. Two trombones. And he played with Jack Carey at certain times.
I never knew Jack Carey. I knew his brother Mutt though.
Yeah well I knew Mutt too. Mutt came down, I mean when I was working on Alamo and Mutt came down one or two times I think. I was working on Alamo with Kaizer. Remember Kaizer?
Oh yes. The Willie Joseph. Willie Joseph. His brother still plays John Joseph. John Joseph.
That's the bass player.
I knew him not very well but I heard him play a couple of times.
Very fine. Very fine bass player. And Willie Joseph was very fine. I worked at Alamo with him for three and a half years. I'm trying to think of what Morris is in a different band.

Well of course we can ask him some more. I didn't get to hear the interview. I wasn't there. But I hope we have most of the information on his life. But I'm wondering also about your other uncle John that played trumpet.
Well Johnny played. He played a long ride. He played with Tick Johnson out of Baton Rouge.
By the way do you know his address or have it at Tick?
No I don't have the address in Baton Rouge but if you get another interview with Morris, Morris has his address. You can get his address from Morris. He played with Tick Johnson.
Tick Johnson, yeah. A lot of people have told me that they played with him. I never got to hear that band.
Well Tick Johnson had a very fine band. Very fine band. Did he play trumpet all his life? All his life we played trumpet. That was his main history. The whole three brothers they played brass.
You know where he studied? No I don't.
I don't. Because he stayed, when my daddy and my uncle moved down here he stayed in the Plast.
Stayed up that way.
Yeah after he left the Plast then he went to Baton Rouge and stayed. But I don't have too much record on him.
You never did play down here then probably at all?
Yeah at times it would take like the bands from Baton Rouge they used to get engaged in here. You know just on his gates they come down and they go back to Baton Rouge.
Is he mostly a dance man rather than brass band? Well he played brass band.
Both of them? Yeah both of them. Dance and brass. He's a very fine trumpet player. Turn those time. I don't think he's playing anymore. He's got a nice age out of him.
I was there a year and a half ago and we couldn't find hardly anyone to interview. No. I knew there must be a few people like your uncle up there but we didn't know. We have a lot of them.
Where to find them at?
The only one we found that day was Willie Foster the guitar. He's in Baton Rouge. He's up there. He's in Baton Rouge. Taking care of his mother.
Well I was wondering where Willie Foster was.
I'm trying to think if their mother has died. She was 106 years old. She must be dead. I think she died since then.
I can say yeah.
Well we've been inquiring about Willie Foster.
Yeah he was up there taking care of her and she'd had a stroke. Fine. But he looked very healthy. He didn't play anymore. No.
He was a great band to play. Very great. Great band to play.
And he was brother Pop Foster the bass player too.

He did. Yeah well Pop Foster was down during the time Pop was living and we played for this night in New Orleans on the. Oh yes. On St. Louis. It was on St. Louis in Royal. And he was down one night. Oh that's alright. It's alright.

It wasn't fair. It wasn't fair. You can turn it off for a second if you like. Yeah. Well if you think of anything you can interrupt later. Alright. And tell us anything later about them. So we can go ahead with your life. Alright. So you say you were born in 1910? I was born in 1910. 1910.
And well I started. Which part of town about do you remember?
I was born back in Carlton.

So on Green Street. Way back in. Way back on Green Street. And I can remember when I was a little kid. Well I always, I always did love music. And we had a piano. And we used to pump the piano. And we used to sing by the piano. Well after I got about, I'd say about 16 or 17 years old and I bought a ukulele. And I started playing ukulele. And from the ukulele I bought a banjo. And well after I got a banjo, I had to work.
Did you take any lessons from anyone or did your father help you?

No. Well by the time I bought the banjo my father died. Oh he did not. That's right. That's until 1925. Around 1927 I think I bought a banjo. And I used to work for a market and used to drive a truck. Well I didn't have time like I wanted, hours was so long so I brought my banjo on the job. And I used to practice on the job. And then I played around, played with a couple of bands and played with some good bands. I had a band myself.
Do you remember your very first band, your first job that you had, about what the job it was or how much you got paid or anything?

The first job I had was across the river. And I played over in Marrero. And during those times I think I made four hours I believe, first job. Well that was plenty of money then. That was pretty good for those days. Yeah. Yeah. Plenty of money in those days. And I played with a band, it was Peter Hicks' band. Peter Hicks was over Marrero. He was a piano player. And I played with him a good while. And then I had some cousins out of the place. You might have heard a trumpet player, let's call him Fat. Then he had a son, that was his nickname, his name was August, and his son played trumpet. And the players used to go up there and play with them. And then after I left there my next band was a man out of St. Rose, Earl Vinnett. Well I stayed around Death Strand about six months, that's when I took left for Poykin. And then we had a band there in St. Rose. And we played around St. Rose and then after a while I came on back to New Orleans. And I played with some bands here.
By the way, do you know about when Dave Perkins died? I don't have any dates on him. We may have someplace.
I don't have the date on Dave Perkins. I think Dave Perkins died, I don't know, I think maybe around the 40s. I'm not sure. Somewhere around the 40s, 39 or 40.
I didn't know he lived that long.
Yeah, he lived that long.
Must have been a pretty old man. He was.
Dave was old, I know he was close to 100 years old. Really? Yeah, close to 100 years old.
Because I heard he played back in the 90s and way back there.

Well during 1932, or 31 or 32 I think I took lessons from him. And I took lessons from Dave about a year anyhow. Well he used to come out to the Central Road, I was driving a truck in Good Hope, he used to come to New Orleans every day. And he came on Sunday mornings and we had the whole band. And he gave the whole band lessons. Well the whole band lessons. Yeah he gave the whole band lessons.
But did you do that at his house or did he come to your house?

No he come to Central Road. The trumpet player, or El Vinnett out of Central Road. He used to come to his house on Sundays and then we'd come down from Death Strand and then we'd take lessons. He'd give us lessons.
Do you remember how he would teach? Did he have a method book for everybody in the band or what did he do?

No he had different method books for them. Well I'll tell you, each person in the band they had to buy a method. You had to buy your own method. Well the method that you had, he had the same method too. Yeah. But what did he do? He'd make you buy the same method that he had.
Do you remember what method you used on your banjo when you started?
I think this method was Morris. Oh yeah. I think it was Morris. Morris method.
It's still a good method I think with that.
Yeah Morris method is a very good method.
I think Professor Mineta uses it I believe now.

Yeah it was Morris. I just remember that name good. And while the trumpet player they had, I think they had this Mike Neal, I think it was a Mike Neal method I think they had. I don't remember that. But yeah they all had different methods. I mean he had different methods to teach each one, different name methods. I mean I think what he did he picked the best method for each instrument that you played. And well we used to take a lesson and as we'd take a lesson that Sunday night we would play it yeah.
Did he coach the whole band together too sometime on whole pieces or how did he?

Well yeah after he finished, everybody had that, took their lesson, well then he'd coach the band. We had the band to play, he'd have a certain number for the band to play together. And each time he'd come out if we played this number good that Sunday, well the next Sunday he'd give us another number to play. What type of music did he teach?
Were they say the Dixieland numbers or the standard numbers or classical?
Dixieland and standard numbers. That's the most he taught. I mean as far as classical, I mean he didn't teach us any classical because most we want to learn.
I meant were there things like say a Sousa March or anything of that kind? No. So popular pieces.
Pieces yeah but no it's, any little simple number that he thought that we could play, the first lesson he'd give us a simple number and the next lesson he'd make it a little harder and so on until.
Did he write out parts for you or have stock arrangements or what?
Well he had some stock arrangements, some parts he wrote out first. He's part of the instrument, he's part of the band.
It's very interesting to know since we'll never get to talk to Dave Perkins to know just what he did, how he taught because he was a famous teacher and he'd like to hear more about
He must have been one of the best. He's just about one of the best because most musicians in New Orleans took lessons from Dave Perkins.
A lot of them did.

Yeah. The older musicians anyhow, they all took lessons from Dave Perkins. And well, then some of them I mean I did went to Professor Humphrey a while but I didn't go there too long. Well I've heard of Jim Humphrey, that's the grandfather of Percy and all that. Yeah that's right, well I didn't go there too long. I went there just a short while.
You did take a few lessons?

A few lessons from him too. The old man Jim. I went to Jim and this Willie Foster, I took lessons from Willie Foster. Well you did, from Willie Foster. I took lessons from Willie Foster. And Willie Foster is a fine teacher too, very fine teacher. I wish he was a teacher now. Probably could.

I mean he looks young enough that he'd retired from some job. He worked up there for some company, I can't think. He just retired a couple of years ago. Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah. So, but he looked very healthy and in good spirits and all.
That's good. Well he was, I mean when he was, of course he was a lot younger, during the, 33, but he was always, I don't know, he always did hold up very well. Yeah.
Very well. I think he's around 70 now. 70 years old. Something pretty close throughout that I think. With his mother living over a hundred he probably will live a long age too.

A hundred himself. That's right. That's right. And I can get back to the subject. Oh yeah. Yeah I can remember certain jobs we played, I mean during those times I mean musicians played, they played a lot. But some of the jobs I mean you get on to a dollar a night. Oh yeah. Yeah we played for a dollar a night.
And then you get tips though I guess.
Well the tip was pretty good sometime yeah. But as time went by things got a little better. But during those times.
During the Depression then when you started out.

That's right. So you had a tough time to start. Had a tough time to start. But you didn't mind because you loved the music so much until it didn't make any difference. I mean of course while we wasn't married, you know young, you didn't need too much money
no more.
A lot of people got through, I know I did too much money no more. That's right.
Can you tell us about any other bands then that you joined, worked with regularly?
Well I worked with, well I worked on that up on the Alamo, you remember the Alamo.
You know I'm trying to think, I don't think I ever.
Well that's where Willie Gilders was working, it was a sort of jitney dance.
Where was that now? On the Canal and, Canal and. The Rondelet, was that the one along in there someplace?
No it was down Drys, the Continuations of Drys. Oh down that far.
Right over Macquarie, that was Tennessee Stowe.
Oh yeah. It was Canal and not Bourbon, I think it was Burgundy. On the downtown side. On the downtown side.
Cause there was another one up on the uptown side.
Yeah well I worked there three and a half years with Willie Gilders.
That's near where the Budweiser was. Yeah where the Budweiser was.

I knew that place. Well after we left there then we moved to Exchange Alley. And I was still working with Willie Gilders. I worked with Willie Gilders about three and a half years. And Poissy Alfre, you know Poissy Alfre? Oh yes. Yeah I worked with Poissy. Poissy was there. And Sidney Carrere, that's the one you don't hear them talk about. No. Sidney Carrere, he's a fine tenor man, he had a brother, Professor Carrere. I think they both passed. I think so too. I never did meet either of them. Yeah well Sidney Carrere was our tenor player. Earl Foster, you know Earl Foster. Oh yes. Yeah well Earl Foster played in the band. And we had Kato, and after Kato we had Charlie Hampton to play. Charlie Hampton played piano with us. Now Charlie Hampton played piano and banjo. That's when you talk of Charlie. He's a very good piano player, a very good banjo player. And I worked, well we worked at Alamo for I'd say about three and a half years. And after I left Alamo, well then I started working around at Caliente. You might remember Caliente. No.
Where was that?
Caliente was on Bienville and Burgundy. You know where the Virginia kitchen? Yeah. Right across from the Virginia kitchen there. I worked at the Caliente. And I worked a lot of spot jobs.
Yeah there was one place I think I know that was called the Magnolia for a while. It was the Magnolia Room.
Yeah. The Magnolia Room. That was the Caliente.
And Paul Barber was working there one summer about fifteen years ago. That's right. That's right.
Well, well, we worked a lot of jobs, a lot of pigments and what not. But the…
Oh, somebody told me you worked once with Ridgely. I worked at Ridgely. I know you worked with Celestan a lot too.
Yeah, I worked at Ridgely too.
Was Celestan with them then or they split up?

Well, Celestan split up then when I worked with Ridgely. I worked with Ridgely, I guess about, I'd say about two years. Working with Ridgely and George McCullin. You remember George? I heard him talk about him.
Very fine trumpet player.

I never got to know him. Yeah, George McCullin was playing trumpet with us. And we had alto player, Joe Harris. And we were actually playing alto with Sam Dutry, tenor player. You might hear talking Sam. That's the old man or the young man?
The young Dutry, yeah.
We had quite a band. I just remember all the fellas in the band. We had quite a band and it was Ridgely. What did he call it then?
Did he call it the Tuxedo then too?

No, he called it Ridgely. Ridgely's band, yeah. Because after they broke up, I think Celestan took the Tuxedo and he just ridgely band after they separated. But the old man is still living. Oh yes, we interviewed him once. He did, uh-huh. He's still living, Ridgely's still living. I was trying to think of some other bands.
When did you start with Celestan?

Oh I started playing with Celestan, I've been with the band now about ten years. Around nineteen, nineteen fifty. With the band ten years. Little better ten years now. And uh, well I mean after, well I joined the band, well before I got in the band, Harrison Verrett was in the band. Yeah. And I worked in Harrison Verrett Police a while, then Harrison Verrett came back in the band and that's Harrison went back again. Well I joined the band back again. I've been with the band ever since. Yeah. And uh, under Papa's leadership and after Papa passed, well then I got, uh, I was under Eddie Pearson. You know Eddie Pearson? Oh yes, being near him. Eddie Pearson leadership. But it was only about two years ago, wasn't it? Just about two years, this summer, it'll be two years. But Papa Celestan was a grand old man, I mean, you couldn't beat him. He was just about one of the best. Yeah he was. He's one of the best you could ever see. And uh, Papa used to, we used to go all the jobs and we'd go, we might go away and stay three or four days. And Papa would get all the boys together. It's one thing about him, he's a kind of man. And he'd tell you, after you get in the band, you go to play someplace. He'd try to keep you together like, just like he was his chair.
You usually travel in that big bus, I used to see that bus. Yeah.
Do you still have that? I still have the bus, I have the bus here.
Oh I used to see it down in front of Paul, not that, Louis Barber.

Oh, Louis Barber. I've been here now, just about, ever since Eddie Pierce. Been having about a year and a half or two years now. But the old man was very fine, Eddie was a very fine manager too. Eddie Pierce was very fine. I did a lot of work with Eddie, Eddie was a good manager, very good manager. And so now the load is on me.
Nobody knew that he had heart trouble, did they? Or did he?
No.
Was it his heart or just started a stroke?

No he had a stroke, he had a stroke in his kidney, I guess after his kidney. That right to Eddie? That his heart went bad. Because he never did complain. Yeah I never knew he was sick or anything wrong with him at all. No, well he didn't like the doctor so that was some of the trouble. Maybe if he went to the doctor he might have lived a couple more years. More checkups. That's right. But Eddie was a fine manager. So I mean I've been having the band about two years now. But I've been doing pretty well with the band.

I'd like to inquire if you have a list of the addresses. We could even put it on the tape and then we can take it off of the tape. If you have the other members of the band that we've interviewed, I don't think I'd ever call him as Fernand as Mr. Walters. Walters, Alba Walters. We had a short interview with him and one with Louis Barbaran. And you I believe are the only members now that we've interviewed. Let's see there's…
Joe Thomas.
Joe Thomas. Somehow we've missed him all the time.
Yeah, Jeanette Kimball.
Jeanette Kimball. I don't have her address.
And I have the new bass player. Well I have a…
Oh yes, I don't know him. Norwood Kimball. Who is the bass player now?
Well Norwood Kimball and I have still two, Steele Davis you see. Out of town I mean Norwood plays out of town job with me and Steele Davis plays a job at any time.
We did interview Sidney Brown about two months ago. He did?
Yeah.
Before he went in the hospital. I understand he's been sick.
I haven't seen him since. He's been like he liked to… His eyesight went bad. Yeah. And he's in church too I guess and almost gave up playing now.
That's right.
He did fine. He still plays in church though. He still plays in church though.
He told me too he was going to play in church.
Yeah, he played in church. So Jeanette is not in town now. She's in Ohio. Oh she's not here now?
No she's not here now.
She stayed at I think 2012 7th Street. And Joe Thomas still St. Anne Street. I have to get his number. I don't have his number.
We have a union book. It's an old book though and half of those addresses people have moved. It's all different.
Yeah they're all there.
You know how musicians move around more than most people.

That's right. That's right. Well still Davis is still on Willow and Sonniac. I don't have a corner over here. Willow and Sonniac. I don't have his address. Not far from here. It's still in the downtown front of town side of the bank. It's right over here. Right over the next corner over there. You know what I asked? Yeah. I said Willow. And Upline. I don't have his number. Willow and Upline. I don't have his address.
Is this other bass player, what's his first name? Norwood Kimball. Norwood. Is he any relation to Jeanette Kimball or the other Kimballs?
I was a husband.
Oh.
Yes.
Husband and wife. Oh sure then. I didn't know his name was Norwood. Yeah. Norwood Kimball.
They were.
They were husband and wife. Yeah. I didn't know the relationship.
He had the same address. 2012 Louis Avenue. Oh yeah. So that's a cool answer then.
Let's see. Are there any other bands that we've skipped in there that you played with?

Well, maybe one. I played with Kit Clayton. He might have heard that. Oh yeah sure I know Kit Clayton. I worked with Kit Clayton. And from Kit Clayton, I worked with George Williams. You heard of George Williams? The drummer? Drummer, yeah. He used to be the paddock. That's right. And I worked with Percy Alfred band too. At the time the old man had the band. Percy Daddy.
Oh Willie, the old Willie.
Old Willie Alfred. Yeah I worked with his band.
We interviewed him too. He's still running.
He's still running. He's still running.
His mind was clear and all when we talked to him about a year ago. I haven't seen him since.
And well I mentioned the old Vinnett band.
Oh if you could tell us. We didn't get to ask Mr. Humphrey. You know he isn't well of course. So we didn't want to pester him with too many questions.
I understand yeah.

But I don't remember if he mentioned your band, that particular one. You might tell us a little bit more about it since we don't want to bother him too much for an interview. You know an old man that age we don't want to keep questioning.

No well during the time I mean he had a fine band. He had one of the number one bands around the world. About when was that? I was around 19, I said 1936. Just around 1936. And his band was going strong. I played quite a few dates with him.
Do you remember who else was in the band who was the cover player?

Well he had his two sons, Percy Offred and Willie. Willie played the clarinet. He had my CD, the piano player. He had my CD. I don't know her but I know her. Yeah, my CD and they had the, let's see what's playing the drum.
Oh yeah.
So you were talking about Willie, the old man Willie Humphrey's band.
Mercy D was playing piano.
Percy played drums for a while I understand.
Yeah he did.
Do you think he might have played in that band?

No he was playing trumpet in that band. We had Syee, Syee was the drummer then. Syee played drums. And we had Mercy D piano, that's right I said Mercy D and myself, and the old man and his two sons, the old man and our friend is two sons.

segments.title: Opening and Albert French's birth in New Orleans
segments.summary: Russell opens the interview at French's home on August 3, 1960; French says he was born November 16, 1910 on Green Street.

segments.title: Father Bob French and uncles Morris and Johnny
segments.summary: French names his father Bob 'Bab' French, a bass tuba player with Kid Rena, his uncles Morris and Johnny, and says his father died in 1925.

segments.title: Father's training with Dave Perkins and his age and family order
segments.summary: His father learned from Dave Perkins, started on tuba, was the oldest brother; Russell asks about bands he played in, including Tuxedo and Eureka.

segments.title: Father's dance and brass band work with Kid Rena; childhood memories
segments.summary: His father played dances at the Bulls and parades; French remembers hearing him as a child, the instrument, and playing in Laplace; Morris in the same band.

segments.title: Kid Rena's style and Shulky following him
segments.summary: Discussion of Kid Rena's high-note style and how Shulky, who followed the band around, played just like him.

segments.title: Members of Kid Rena's band and clarinetist Zeb
segments.summary: French lists the band: Chester Zarder on bass, Zeb on clarinet, Morris, his father, and drummer Joe Rena; they discuss Zeb's age and origins.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong on television and French imitating his singing
segments.summary: Chat about an Armstrong television interview and French imitating Armstrong's singing when young, while playing ukulele.

segments.title: Uncle Morris: arrival, other bands, Jack Carey, and the Alamo
segments.summary: Morris's origin in Laplace, his bands including Taft Kroon and Jack Carey, and French's work at the Alamo with Willie and John Joseph.

segments.title: Uncle Johnny French in Baton Rouge and Willie Foster
segments.summary: Johnny played trumpet with Tick Johnson in Baton Rouge in dance and brass bands; talk turns to Willie Foster and his mother, and Pop Foster.

segments.title: Starting on ukulele and banjo, Green Street
segments.summary: French loved music, pumped the piano, bought a ukulele at 16-17 then a banjo around 1927, practicing on his truck-driving job.

segments.title: First job in Marrero and early bands
segments.summary: His first job was across the river in Marrero with Peter Hicks, then bands with cousins and Earl Vinnett in St. Rose before returning to New Orleans.

segments.title: Dave Perkins's death and Sunday band lessons
segments.summary: French recalls Perkins dying around 1940, nearly 100, and his Sunday band lessons around 1931-32 at Central Road.

segments.title: Perkins's teaching method, method books and repertoire
segments.summary: Each player bought a method book, such as the Morris banjo method; Perkins coached the band on Dixieland and standard numbers and used stock arrangements.

segments.title: Lessons with Jim Humphrey and Willie Foster
segments.summary: French took a few lessons from Professor Jim Humphrey and from Willie Foster, with Russell on Foster's health and age.

segments.title: Low pay in Depression-era jobs
segments.summary: Jobs paid about a dollar a night with tips during the Depression, but loving the music made it bearable.

segments.title: Willie Gilders's band at the Alamo, Exchange Alley and Caliente
segments.summary: French worked about three and a half years with Willie Gilders at the Alamo and Exchange Alley with Sidney Carrere, Earl Foster and Charlie Hampton, then at Caliente.

segments.title: Playing with Ridgley after the Tuxedo split with Celestin
segments.summary: French worked about two years with Ridgley's band, with George McCullin, Joe Harris and Sam Dutrey, after Ridgley and Celestin separated.

segments.title: Joining Papa Celestin's band and leadership under Eddie Pierson
segments.summary: French joined Celestin around 1950, recalls travelling with the band and bus, Celestin's character, and Eddie Pierson's management after Celestin died.

segments.title: Celestin's illness and death, Pierson's management
segments.summary: They discuss Celestin's stroke and heart trouble, his dislike of doctors, and French now leading the band.

segments.title: Celestin band members and their addresses
segments.summary: Russell asks for addresses of band members; French names Joe Thomas, Jeanette and Norwood Kimball, Steele Davis and Sidney Brown.

segments.title: Other bands: Kid Clayton, George Williams and old Willie Humphrey
segments.summary: French mentions working with Kid Clayton, George Williams, and the old Willie Humphrey band.

segments.title: The Humphrey band around 1936 and its members
segments.summary: French describes the Humphrey band of about 1936, with sons Percy and Willie, piano and drums, and Percy on trumpet.
